summary.value: The paper proposes MoE-GS, a Mixture-of-Experts framework for dynamic Gaussian splatting that adaptively combines heterogeneous deformation priors to improve dynamic novel view synthesis. It introduces a Volume-aware Pixel Router that learns per-Gaussian, time- and view-dependent weights and splats them through the differentiable rasterizer to obtain per-pixel gates for blending expert renderings (Section 3.2; Figure 3), trained in a two-stage pipeline where experts are first optimized and then frozen before router training (Figure 2; Appendix C.1–C.3). To offset MoE overhead, the authors develop single-pass multi-expert rendering and gate-aware Gaussian pruning (Section 3.3; Eq. 9–10), and further propose a distillation scheme that transfers MoE performance to individual experts using router-weighted pseudo-labels (Section 3.4; Eq. 11). Experiments on N3V and Technicolor show consistent state-of-the-art performance and robust generalization across scenes, with efficiency gains from pruning and single-pass rendering (Tables 1–3, 5). The router design outperforms pixel-only and volume-only routing variants (Table 4; Figure 5), and the method yields improved multi-view geometric stability via a post-hoc fused Gaussian model (Appendix E; Figure 10). Overall, MoE-GS is presented as the first integration of MoE into dynamic Gaussian splatting, offering adaptive, spatially and temporally coherent expert blending.

strengths.value:
1. Clear problem motivation with empirical evidence. Figure 1 (a–c) convincingly shows scene-, space-, and time-dependent performance variability across dynamic GS methods, justifying the need for adaptive expert selection rather than a single deformation prior.

2. First MoE formulation tailored to dynamic Gaussian splatting. The paper introduces a domain-specific MoE design that operates on expert-rendered images while grounding routing in volumetric signals (Section 3.2), which is a creative and well-placed synthesis of MoE with explicit 3D representations.

3. Volume-aware Pixel Router with differentiable weight splatting. The router bridges 3D Gaussian attributes and 2D gating by learning per-Gaussian, time- and view-dependent weights and “rasterization-based weight splatting” (Eqs. 6–8; Figure 3; Figure 6). This hybrid design is technically neat and addresses optimization challenges of pure pixel or pure volume routing.

4. Strong ablation validating the router design. The proposed router substantially outperforms Pixel Router and Volume Router baselines (Table 4: PSNR 33.23 vs. 31.12/32.05; Figure 5 shows sharper details), directly supporting the architectural choice rather than relying on end-to-end gains only.

5. Principled efficiency improvements beyond naïve MoE. Single-Pass Multi-Expert Rendering shares projection/visibility across experts (Eq. 9; Section 3.3), and Gate-Aware Gaussian Pruning uses gradients of gating weights w.r.t. per-Gaussian weights (Eq. 10) to prune with a meaningful importance signal. Together they lift FPS and reduce memory while preserving quality (Table 5: 68 FPS with full model vs. 36/40/60 in ablations; Table 3: pruning raises FPS from 44 to 83–101 with minimal PSNR drop).

6. Distillation that leverages router-weighted pseudo-labels. The loss in Eq. 11 uses G′ as confidence to transfer MoE strengths back to single experts, yielding consistent gains across methods (Table 7; Table 11). This is a practical pathway to deploy near-MoE quality without architectural changes.

7. Geometry-aware analysis and quantitative 3D evaluation. The lifting of pixel gates back to Gaussians and post-hoc fusion (Appendix E.1–E.2; Eq. 15) is conceptually elegant, and the multi-view depth consistency metric (Appendix E.3; Figure 10) shows improved geometric stability, indicating benefits beyond photometric PSNR.

8. Comprehensive experimental validation across datasets and regimes. Consistent state-of-the-art on N3V and Technicolor (Tables 1–2), with additional evaluations on HyperNeRF showing transfer to monocular settings (Table 10). The gating visualizations (Figure 4) corroborate spatially coherent routing aligned with expert strengths.

9. Training-efficiency insights and robustness. The partial budget study shows MoE-GS remains strong even with 10–20% expert training time (Table 6), and the router adds “less than 5% computation” (Section 4.2). Stability across repeated runs (Appendix G; Table 12) demonstrates the gains are structural, not due to training variance.

10. Reproducibility and engineering clarity. The two-stage training protocol (Appendix C.1–C.3), fixed expert sets for all experiments (Section 4.1), and detailed rendering implementation (Appendix C.4) make the work easy to follow and reimplement. The discussion of rejected alternatives (multi-GPU, sequential offloading in Appendix C.4) shows careful systems thinking.

11. Insightful analysis of expert inductive biases. Appendix F explains why different experts excel in different motion regimes (e.g., “HexPlane canonical deformation” yielding smooth low-motion trajectories vs. “keyframe interpolation” enabling irregular motion), strengthening the conceptual rationale for MoE-GS.

12. Practical efficiency–quality tradeoffs quantified. Table 3 and Table 5 present concrete PSNR/FPS/memory numbers and pruning ratios, providing actionable guidance for deploying N=2–3 experts with high efficiency.

Overall, the paper combines a clear, data-driven motivation with a novel, well-specified router, principled efficiency mechanisms, and thorough, geometry-aware evaluation. The breadth and depth of analyses (Sections 3.2–3.4; Tables 1–7; Appendix E–H) demonstrate strong execution and practical significance.

weaknesses.value:
1. Efficiency claims are relative to naïve MoE, not to single-expert SOTA. In Table 3, MoE-GS (N=2) is far slower than Ex4DGS (44 FPS vs. 120) and uses substantially more memory (878.7 MB vs. 122.8 MB). Even with 55–75% pruning, FPS and memory remain inferior or only comparable to the fastest expert, while PSNR gains are modest. Please (a) report FLOPs/throughput vs. PSNR trade-offs against the best single expert per scene, (b) quantify memory vs. pruning curves, and (c) include temporal stability metrics to ensure pruning does not induce flicker.

2. Potential inconsistency introduced by Single-Pass Multi-Expert Rendering. Equation (9) accumulates colors using a global transmittance Tj(u) over the concatenated Gaussians of all experts. This differs from per-expert rasterization where Tj is computed within each expert’s set. Although the text states “without altering the rendering formulation” (Section 3.3), the cross-expert occlusion in Tj can change expert-specific outputs before routing. Please measure the deviation between single-pass and true multi-pass rendering (e.g., per-pixel ΔPSNR/SSIM and visual diffs), and discuss any bias this introduces into the gates and pruning.

3. Fixed expert set and limited exploration of scalability. All main results use a single, predetermined set of up to four experts (Section 4.1). This leaves open whether the method scales to different expert families, larger banks, or multiple variants per family. Provide (a) results with alternative expert pools (e.g., swapping one expert type), (b) scaling studies beyond N=4 with distillation to show diminishing returns/compute curves, and (c) analysis of gate entropy/diversity across space/time to verify non-trivial usage when the pool grows.

4. Fairness concerns in baseline training and data splits. Table 1 marks STG with † trained on a 150-frame split, which may disadvantage it on N3V relative to other methods. Since MoE-GS uses STG as an expert and also competes against it, ensure equal training budgets/splits across all baselines, or report a matched comparison where all methods use the same frame budget. Otherwise, the relative gains may partially reflect unequal training conditions.

5. Router expressivity vs. complexity trade-offs are underexplored. The Volume-aware Pixel Router uses low-dimensional per-Gaussian weights [w, wdir, t·wtime] and a lightweight MLP Φ (Eqs. 6–8; Appendix C.3). While effective, it may be capacity-limited for challenging, view-dependent dynamics. Please add ablations varying router capacity (e.g., higher-dimensional per-Gaussian embeddings or deeper Φ), and report how routing entropy, PSNR, and FPS change to justify the chosen design.

6. Lack of oracle and simpler ensemble baselines to bound the problem. To contextualize MoE-GS’s effectiveness, include “oracle” upper bounds: (a) per-frame best expert and (b) per-patch best expert (non-causal, ground-truth selected). Also add simple ensembles (uniform average of experts; fixed per-expert scalar weights learned per-scene). This will quantify the headroom for routing and demonstrate that the learned router outperforms simpler mixtures beyond the router-variant ablations (Table 4).

7. Distillation scope and costs are only partially quantified. The MoE-guided distillation improves experts (Table 7; Table 11), but the training overhead and wall-clock gains at deployment are not reported. For completeness, provide (a) distillation training time vs. vanilla retraining (per expert), (b) inference FPS/memory for distilled experts relative to original ones, and (c) results on more scenes where gains for STG and Ex4DGS are modest (Table 7) to characterize when distillation meaningfully helps.

8. Pruning criterion may be brittle under saturated gates. Gate-Aware Gaussian Pruning uses the gradient norm of G′ w.r.t. wper (Eq. 10). When gates saturate, informative Gaussians might show small gradients and be pruned. Please compare against volumetric-contribution–based scores (e.g., Eq. 12 Ck,j or accumulated α) and hybrid criteria, and report quality vs. threshold curves (PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS and temporal metrics) to establish robustness.

9. Geometry evaluation is post-hoc and not tied to the deployed model. The improved Multi-view Depth Consistency (MDC) is measured on a fused Gaussian model formed by scaling opacities with responsibilities (Appendix E.2; Eq. 15) rather than on the actual MoE rendering path. Report (a) MDC for each individual expert and for the MoE-rendered depth (if available) to connect the metric to the deployed pathway, and (b) photometric performance of the fused model to show it does not trade geometry for appearance.

10. Limited discussion of failure modes and when MoE-GS underperforms. While average gains are clear (Tables 1–2), there are scenes where improvements are small, and N=4 does not always beat N=3 (Table 1). Provide per-scene analyses linking motions (Appendix F) to router behavior, highlighting cases where routing collapses to a single expert or experts conflict, and propose mitigations (e.g., diversity regularization, calibration losses on gates).

questions.value:
1. Single-pass rendering equivalence and bias
   - Section 3.3/Eq. 9 computes expert-specific colors Ck(u) with a single global transmittance Tj(u) over the concatenated Gaussians, whereas the “true” multi-pass MoE would compute T within each expert and then blend I_Ek by G′k (Eq. 8). Please quantify the deviation between single-pass and multi-pass: per-pixel error maps, ΔPSNR/SSIM over N3V/Technicolor, and any gating distribution shifts. If they are not equivalent, can you derive conditions when they match and discuss whether single-pass introduces cross-expert occlusion that biases pruning or router learning?

2. Fairness of STG training on N3V
   - Table 1 marks STG with † (150-frame split). Since STG is both a baseline and an expert inside MoE-GS, could you provide a matched setting where all methods (and the STG expert) use the same number of frames? Alternatively, report MoE-GS results when the STG expert is constrained to the same 150-frame budget as the baseline to rule out data-budget-induced gains.

3. Router capacity and feature design
   - The Volume-aware Pixel Router uses 3 scalars per Gaussian and a lightweight Φ (Eqs. 6–8; Appendix C.3). Could you provide an ablation that:
     a) Increases per-Gaussian embedding dimensionality (e.g., 8–16D) and/or deepens Φ, and reports PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS and FPS?
     b) Augments inputs with readily available volumetric signals (e.g., per-pixel depth, transmittance, accumulated opacity) to test whether more explicit geometry cues help over w2D, wdir2D, wtime2D and r(u)?

4. Gate entropy and expert utilization
   - To establish that the router meaningfully uses multiple experts (not collapsing), please report gate entropy distributions over pixels and time, and per-expert pixel coverage on N3V/Technicolor (also see Figure 4). A visualization of temporal evolution would help validate the motivation in Figure 1c.

5. Oracle and simple ensemble baselines
   - To contextualize the achievable headroom and the router’s benefit beyond Table 4, could you include:
     a) Per-frame and per-patch “oracle” upper bounds (selecting the best expert against GT).
     b) Simple ensembles (uniform average of experts; per-scene learned scalar weights). This would bound the achievable gains and show the router’s added value.

6. Scaling beyond the fixed expert pool
   - Section 4.1 fixes expert sets for N=2–4. Please provide:
     a) Results swapping one expert type (e.g., replacing 4DGaussians with another HexPlane-based variant) to show robustness to pool composition.
     b) Limited scaling beyond N=4 using distillation (Section 3.4), reporting returns vs. compute/memory, to demonstrate practical saturation points.

7. Distillation costs and deployment gains
   - Section 3.4 and Tables 7/11 show quality gains, but the training and deployment economics are unclear. Please report:
     a) Distillation wall-clock vs. vanilla retraining per expert.
     b) Inference FPS/memory of distilled experts vs. their original versions.
     c) How λ in Eq. 11 is selected; provide sensitivity curves and whether temperature/label smoothing are used for stability.

8. Pruning criterion robustness
   - Gate-aware pruning (Eq. 10) uses ∥∂G′k/∂wper_i∥ averaged over views. Clarify how k is handled (max/mean over experts or summed?), and whether gradients are collected at a stable router epoch to avoid early-phase noise. Please compare against volumetric-contribution scores (Eq. 12 or accumulated α) and a hybrid metric, and plot PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS vs. τ along with a temporal stability metric to ensure no flicker.

9. Geometry evaluation on the deployed path
   - Appendix E evaluates MDC on a post-hoc fused model (Eq. 15). Could you also report:
     a) MDC for the actual MoE renderings (e.g., from depth of the blended RGBs or by fusing per-expert depths with G′k)?
     b) Photometric metrics of the fused model to show geometry gains do not significantly trade off appearance?
     c) MDC per individual expert (for context alongside Figure 10)?

10. Quantifying router overhead and training efficiency
   - Section 4.2 states the router adds “less than 5% computation.” Please provide exact numbers (GPU-hours and peak memory) for Stage 2 relative to Stage 1, and a breakdown of router compute (weight splatting vs. Φ).

11. Partial-budget training details
   - Table 6 shows strong results at 10–20% of expert budgets. Please clarify:
     a) Whether learning-rate schedules/iterations were proportionally shortened or truncated.
     b) If early stopping checkpoints were tuned per expert to avoid under/overfitting biases.
     c) Whether reduced-budget experts degrade router training stability (e.g., more entropy or noisier gates).

12. Time normalization and sequence length
   - In Eq. 6, time appears as t·wtime. How is t normalized across scenes (e.g., [0,1]) and sequence lengths? Does the router generalize to longer sequences or variable frame rates without re-scaling? Any evidence on cross-sequence transfer?

13. Stability across runs and calibration
   - Appendix G/Table 12 shows run-to-run variability. Do you apply any calibration (e.g., gate temperature) or diversity regularizers to stabilize routing across seeds? Reporting mean±std of PSNR and entropy across 5 runs for MoE-GS would help assess robustness.

14. Failure cases and N=3 vs. N=4 regressions
   - In Table 1, N=4 slightly underperforms N=3 on Sear Steak and Average. Can you analyze where extra experts hurt (e.g., gate confusion, over-pruning, occlusion in single-pass rendering) and suggest mitigations (entropy regularization, gate sparsity, curriculum)?

15. Temporal stability metrics
   - Beyond PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS (Tables 1–2, 4–5), please add a temporal stability measure (e.g., frame-to-frame consistency using optical flow–warped errors) to show that pruning and MoE blending do not introduce flicker, especially after aggressive 75% pruning (Table 3).

16. Memory accounting methodology
   - Tables 3 and 5 report memory usage (e.g., 878.7 vs. 270). Please specify measurement protocol (allocated VRAM peak, excluding/including expert buffers, router buffers, fused weights) and whether single-pass reduces peak memory via shared buffers.

17. Clarify router inputs and initialization
   - Appendix C.3 says wdir and wtime are initialized near-zero. Are base weights w also near-zero or learned from a prior (e.g., per-expert scalar)? Any normalization or clipping during splatting to prevent scale explosions when added residually in Eq. 7?

18. Alternative inference via fused Gaussians
   - Given the promising MDC of the fused model (Appendix E), could this be a practical deployment path (single explicit GS model)? Please report its FPS/memory and photometric performance relative to running MoE-GS or a distilled expert.

19. Additional monocular evaluation details
   - Table 10 shows MoE-GS (N=2) improves on HyperNeRF. Please clarify training specifics (camera/pose handling, sequence length) and whether router gating remains stable with the sparser supervision typical of monocular settings.

20. Reproducibility and release plan
   - Given the multi-component system (experts, router, pruning, single-pass renderer, distillation), will you release code, trained MoE checkpoints, and scripts for the post-hoc fusion and MDC evaluation (Appendix E) to ensure the community can validate the pipeline end-to-end?
